extraction.name: SQuAD
extraction.description: The Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD) is a reading comprehension dataset consisting of 100,000+ questions posed by crowdworkers on a set of Wikipedia articles, where the answer to each question is a segment of text (span) from the corresponding reading passage. SQuAD contains 107,785 question-answer pairs on 536 articles.
extraction.creator: Pranav Rajpurkar, Jian Zhang, Konstantin Lopyrev, Percy Liang
extraction.citeAs: Rajpurkar, P., Zhang, J., Lopyrev, K., & Liang, P. (2016). SQuAD: 100,000+ Questions for Machine Comprehension of Text. arXiv:1606.05250.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was collected in three stages: (1) curating passages from Wikipedia articles, (2) crowdsourcing question-answer pairs on those passages, and (3) obtaining additional answers for the development and test sets to enable robust evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: 2.6% of questions in development and test sets were marked unanswerable by at least one additional crowdworker.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Top 10,000 articles of English Wikipedia retrieved using Project Nayuki's Wikipedia internal PageRanks, from which 536 articles were sampled uniformly at random. Individual paragraphs were extracted, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters, resulting in 23,215 paragraphs.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Individual paragraphs were extracted from 536 Wikipedia articles, stripping away images, figures, tables, and discarding paragraphs shorter than 500 characters. The result was 23,215 paragraphs partitioned randomly into training set (80%), development set (10%), and test set (10%).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Crowdworkers were tasked with asking and answering up to 5 questions on the content of each paragraph. Questions had to be entered in a text field, and answers had to be highlighted in the paragraph. Tasks contained sample paragraphs with examples of good and bad questions. Workers were encouraged to ask questions in their own words, without copying word phrases from the paragraph; copy-paste functionality was disabled. Workers spent 4 minutes per paragraph and were paid $9/hour. For additional answer collection, crowdworkers were shown questions with paragraphs and asked to select the shortest span answering the question.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Daemo platform with Amazon Mechanical Turk as its backend
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Human performance was assessed by treating the second answer to each question as human prediction, keeping other answers as ground truth. Human performance on test set was 77.0% exact match and 86.8% F1. Mismatch occurred mostly due to inclusion/exclusion of non-essential phrases rather than fundamental disagreements.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: At least 3 answers per question in development and test sets (1 original + at least 2 additional). Training set questions have 1 answer.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Crowdworkers required to have 97% HIT acceptance rate, minimum of 1000 HITs, and located in the United States or Canada.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: Stanford CoreNLP (for constituency parses, POS tags, NER tags, and dependency parses used in analysis and feature extraction)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Dataset freely available at https://stanford-qa.com. Code, data, and experiments available on CodaLab platform. Paper references v1.0 and v1.1 of the dataset, indicating versioning.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Questions with span-based answers are more constrained than more interpretative questions found in advanced standardized tests. The effective accuracy ceiling is limited because only 77.3% of correct answers in the development set are constituents in the constituency parse. Answers must be spans of text from the passage rather than free-form or requiring multi-document reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, and testing of reading comprehension / machine comprehension models. Training set (80%), development set (10%), test set (10%). Used to evaluate systems that must select the answer from all possible spans in a passage.
